motion_movie.move: Cut the 3 by 3 and 4 by 4 squares into 25 loose unit squares and slide them one at a time into the 5 by 5 square on the hypotenuse.
motion_movie.freeze_frame: The last unit square drops in and the 5 by 5 square is exactly full. That picture becomes 9 + 16 = 25.
motion_movie.talk_back: The area of the square on the hypotenuse equals ___ because ___.

part_d.gemini_sim_prompt:
You are building an interactive teaching simulation inside this chat / Canvas.

AUDIENCE: Grade 8 Mathematics. TEKS 8.6C.
GOAL: Students must SEE the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the combined area of the squares on the two legs. They must not only compute.

REQUIRED CONTROLS
- Draggable vertices, so the student can pull leg a and leg b and watch all three squares resize live.
- Draggable unit squares the student can move from the leg squares into the hypotenuse square.
- Live labels using right triangle, leg, hypotenuse, area, square unit.
- A talk-back stem on screen: "The area of the square on the hypotenuse equals ___ because ___."
- A misconception mode that can display: the hypotenuse is the two legs added, 3 + 4 = 7; the relationship holds for any triangle, not only a right one; squaring is a keystroke rather than the area of a square on that side

REQUIRED VISUAL
- A right triangle with an actual square drawn on all three sides, so a squared, b squared and c squared are AREAS the student can count.
- Faint grid lines inside every square so unit squares are countable.
- An area bar that updates: 9 + 16 = 25.
- An obtuse mode where the tiles visibly fail to fill the largest square.

CONSTRAINTS
- Start on a clean 3-4-5 triangle so the areas are 9, 16 and 25.
- Do not show the algebraic form until after the tiles have filled the square.
- Eighth-grade readable. No clutter. Do not invent extra TEKS.
- If you cannot draw the model, say so and draw the next-best area model. Do not ship a calculator.

notebooklm_packs.title: Seeing the Pythagorean Theorem as Area
notebooklm_packs.teks_block: 8.6C Use models and diagrams to explain the Pythagorean theorem
notebooklm_packs.source_doc_markdown:
VIDEO STEERING: Cinematic classroom explainer, 3-6 minutes, no background music louder than the voice, on-screen labels for every academic vocabulary word the first time it is spoken, freeze on the model before any formula appears.

# Seeing the Pythagorean Theorem as Area

Grade 8 Mathematics. Posted TEKS 8.6C, use models and diagrams to explain the Pythagorean theorem.

## Objective and how mastery is shown

Students explain the Pythagorean theorem using a model in which each side of a right triangle carries a square, and the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the combined area of the squares on the two legs. Mastery is shown when a student builds or draws the three squares, states the areas in square units, and explains in their own words why the two smaller areas must fill the larger one. A student who writes a correct number without an area model has not yet met this standard, because 8.6C is about explaining with models and diagrams, not about computing a missing side.

## The motion movie, in four beats

Scene. A right triangle is drawn on centimetre grid paper with legs of 3 and 4 units. The right angle is marked with a small box. Three paper squares are cut to sit exactly on the three sides: a 3 by 3 square, a 4 by 4 square, and a 5 by 5 square. Each square is a real object the class can pick up, not a label.

Move. The 3 by 3 square is cut into 9 unit squares and the 4 by 4 square is cut into 16 unit squares. Students slide those 25 loose unit squares, one at a time, into the square resting on the hypotenuse. They keep going until the large square is full. Nothing is left over and no gap remains.

Freeze frame. Hold the moment the last unit square drops into place and the 5 by 5 square is exactly covered. That picture is the equation. Only after the class has looked at the full square does the line 9 + 16 = 25 appear, and only after that does the general form a squared plus b squared equals c squared appear.

Talk-back. A student says: the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the area of the square on one leg plus the area of the square on the other leg.

## One fully worked example

Worked example: a right triangle with legs of 3 units and 4 units. Step 1, build the square on the first leg. Its side is 3 units, so its area is 3 times 3, which is 9 square units. Count the 9 unit squares on the grid to confirm it. Step 2, build the square on the second leg. Its side is 4 units, so its area is 4 times 4, which is 16 square units. Count the 16 unit squares. Step 3, build the square on the hypotenuse. Its side is 5 units, so its area is 5 times 5, which is 25 square units. Step 4, test the claim by moving area. Take all 9 unit squares from the first square and all 16 unit squares from the second, which is 25 unit squares in total, and tile them into the 25 square units of the largest square. They fit exactly. Step 5, write what the picture showed: 9 + 16 = 25, and in general a squared plus b squared equals c squared, where a and b are the legs and c is the hypotenuse.

The diagram to describe on screen: a right triangle sits in the centre with the right angle at the lower left. A shaded square hangs below the horizontal leg labelled 16 square units. A shaded square sits to the left of the vertical leg labelled 9 square units. A larger square rests on the slanted side, labelled 25 square units. Faint grid lines run through all three squares so every unit square is countable.

## The misconception this visual kills

The wrong idea is that the hypotenuse is simply the two legs added together, so a triangle with legs 3 and 4 would have a hypotenuse of 7. It survives when students only ever see the letters a, b and c and never see area. The model kills it because a square built on a side of 7 would have an area of 49 square units, and the class has just watched only 25 unit squares come off the legs. There is no way to fill 49 with 25, and the gap is visible on the grid rather than argued about.

A second wrong idea is that the relationship holds for any triangle. Tilting the triangle so the right angle opens past ninety degrees makes the square on the longest side grow while the leg squares stay the same, and the tiles no longer fill it. The right angle is the condition, not decoration.

## Talk-back stem and an acceptable answer

Stem: the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals ___ because ___. An acceptable answer: the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals 25 square units because the 9 unit squares from one leg and the 16 unit squares from the other leg filled it exactly, with nothing left over. A student who says c equals 5 because I used the formula has computed, not explained, and the narrator should return to the tiles.

## One STAAR-flavored check

A right triangle has legs measuring 6 units and 8 units. Squares are drawn on all three sides. What is the area of the square drawn on the hypotenuse? The correct answer is 100 square units, because 36 plus 64 is 100. A choice of 14 square units catches the student who added the two side lengths instead of the areas. A choice of 48 square units catches the student who multiplied the legs, which finds twice the area of the triangle rather than the square on the hypotenuse. A choice of 10 square units catches the student who found the length of the hypotenuse and stopped, reporting a length where an area was asked for.

## Closing line for the narrator

The theorem is not a formula to remember. It is a statement about area you can watch happen on grid paper.

notebooklm_packs.teks_block: 8.7C Use the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse to solve problems
notebooklm_packs.source_doc_markdown:
VIDEO STEERING: Cinematic classroom explainer, 3-6 minutes, no background music louder than the voice, on-screen labels for every academic vocabulary word the first time it is spoken, freeze on the model before any formula appears.

# Testing for a Right Angle: the Converse

Grade 8 Mathematics. Posted TEKS 8.7C, use the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse to solve problems.

## Objective and how mastery is shown

Students decide whether a triangle is a right triangle by comparing the area of the square on the longest side against the combined areas of the squares on the other two sides. Mastery is shown when a student tests a set of three side lengths, states whether the triangle is right, and justifies the decision with areas rather than with a remembered rule. The theorem says that if a triangle is right, the areas balance. The converse runs the other way: if the areas balance, the triangle is right. Students who cannot say which direction they are using will misuse both.

## The motion movie, in four beats

Scene. Three strips of card, 6, 8 and 10 units long, lie on grid paper beside three paper squares of area 36, 64 and 100 square units. The strips are hinged at their ends so the triangle can open and close.

Move. Close the hinge until the triangle is narrow and open it slowly. As the angle between the two shorter strips opens, the square on the longest side is rebuilt each time to match the gap between the far ends. The class watches its area climb.

Freeze frame. Hold the instant the square on the longest side reads exactly 100 square units, the same as 36 plus 64. A paper right angle slid into the corner fits exactly. That coincidence is the converse.

Talk-back. A student says: this is a right triangle because 36 plus 64 equals 100, so the areas balance.

## One fully worked example

Worked example: are 9, 12 and 15 the sides of a right triangle? Step 1, find the longest side. It is 15, so the square on it would have an area of 15 times 15, which is 225 square units. Step 2, square the two shorter sides. 9 times 9 is 81 square units and 12 times 12 is 144 square units. Step 3, combine the two smaller areas. 81 plus 144 is 225 square units. Step 4, compare. 225 equals 225, so the two smaller squares would tile the largest one exactly, and the triangle is right. Step 5, test a set that fails. For 9, 12 and 16 the largest square is 256 square units while 81 plus 144 is only 225 square units. The tiles fall 31 square units short, so the angle must have opened past ninety degrees and the triangle is obtuse.

The diagram to describe on screen: three hinged strips forming a triangle, with a shaded square built outward on each side. The two smaller squares are labelled 81 and 144 square units. The largest square is labelled 225 square units, and a small paper right-angle marker sits in the corner between the two shorter sides.

## The misconception this visual kills

The wrong idea is that any three lengths that look reasonable make a right triangle, or that checking is a matter of eyeballing the corner. Students accept 9, 12 and 16 because it is close to 9, 12 and 15. The model kills it because a 31 square unit gap is visible on the grid, and no amount of squinting closes it.

A second wrong idea is direction. Students apply the theorem to a triangle nobody has said is right, and compute a side that does not exist. The converse is the tool for deciding; the theorem is the tool for measuring once the decision is made.

## Talk-back stem and an acceptable answer

Stem: this triangle is or is not right because ___. An acceptable answer: this is not a right triangle because the square on the longest side is 256 square units but the other two squares only give 225 square units, so they cannot fill it. A student who says it does not look right has not used the areas and should be sent back to the grid.

## One STAAR-flavored check

Which set of side lengths forms a right triangle? The correct answer is 7, 24 and 25, because 49 plus 576 is 625, which is 25 times 25. A choice of 5, 6 and 7 catches the student who assumes consecutive numbers work, since 25 plus 36 is 61 and not 49. A choice of 8, 15 and 16 catches the student who is close but never checks, since 64 plus 225 is 289 and not 256. A choice of 3, 4 and 6 catches the student who remembers 3-4-5 and changes one number without retesting.

## Closing line for the narrator

The corner does not tell you it is right. The areas do.

VIDEO STEERING: Cinematic classroom explainer, 3-6 minutes, no background music louder than the voice, on-screen labels for every academic vocabulary word the first time it is spoken, freeze on the model before any formula appears.

# Distance on the Coordinate Plane

Grade 8 Mathematics. Posted TEKS 8.7D, determine the distance between two points on a coordinate plane using the Pythagorean Theorem.

## Objective and how mastery is shown

Students find the distance between two points by dropping a right triangle onto the coordinate plane, using the horizontal and vertical gaps as the legs. Mastery is shown when a student draws the triangle, labels both legs by counting grid units, and explains that the distance is the hypotenuse rather than the sum of the two gaps. A student who produces a number without the triangle has not shown this standard, because 8.7D is about seeing the triangle that is already hiding in the grid.

## The motion movie, in four beats

Scene. A coordinate plane on grid paper. Two points are marked with counters: point A at (1, 2) and point B at (5, 5). A length of string is stretched between them.

Move. Walk one counter horizontally from A until it sits directly under B, counting 4 units aloud, then walk it vertically up to B, counting 3 units. The path traced is two sides of a right triangle. The string stays stretched along the third side the whole time.

Freeze frame. Hold the moment the horizontal leg reads 4, the vertical leg reads 3, and the string lies along the hypotenuse. That picture is the triangle, and the distance is the string.

Talk-back. A student says: the legs are 4 and 3, so the distance is the hypotenuse, not 7.

## One fully worked example

Worked example: find the distance from A at (1, 2) to B at (5, 5). Step 1, find the horizontal gap. From x equals 1 to x equals 5 is 4 units. Count the grid squares; do not subtract carelessly. Step 2, find the vertical gap. From y equals 2 to y equals 5 is 3 units. Step 3, draw the right triangle. The horizontal gap and the vertical gap meet at (5, 2), and that corner is the right angle. Step 4, build the squares. The square on the horizontal leg has an area of 16 square units and the square on the vertical leg has an area of 9 square units. Step 5, combine and read the hypotenuse. 16 plus 9 is 25 square units, so the square on the hypotenuse has an area of 25 square units and its side is 5 units. The distance from A to B is 5 units. Walking the two legs took 7 units, which is why the straight path is shorter.

The diagram to describe on screen: a coordinate plane with A at (1, 2) and B at (5, 5), a dashed horizontal segment to (5, 2), a dashed vertical segment up to B, a right-angle box at (5, 2), and a solid segment from A to B labelled 5 units.

## A second case worth showing

Not every pair of points needs a triangle. Take C at (3, 6) and D at (9, 6). Both sit on the same horizontal line, so the vertical gap is 0 and the horizontal gap is 6. There is no triangle to drop, and the distance is simply 6 units. Students should meet this case early, because a student who has only ever seen slanted pairs will invent a triangle that is not there and report something other than 6. The same holds for two points sharing an x-coordinate: count the vertical gap and stop. The triangle is a tool for the slanted case, not a ritual to perform every time.

## The misconception this visual kills

The wrong idea is that the distance is the horizontal gap plus the vertical gap, so 4 plus 3 gives 7. It comes from counting the walk instead of measuring the flight. The model kills it because the string is visibly shorter than the two dashed legs laid end to end, and every student can see that a straight line beats a detour.

A second wrong idea is subtracting the coordinates in the wrong order and reporting a negative leg. A leg is a length. Counting grid squares makes a negative impossible.

## Talk-back stem and an acceptable answer

Stem: the distance is ___ and not ___ because ___. An acceptable answer: the distance is 5 and not 7 because 4 and 3 are the legs of the right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse, which is always shorter than walking both legs.

## One STAAR-flavored check

What is the distance between the points (2, 1) and (10, 7)? The correct answer is 10 units, because the legs are 8 and 6, and 64 plus 36 is 100. A choice of 14 units catches the student who added the two gaps instead of using the triangle. A choice of 48 units catches the student who multiplied the legs. A choice of 100 units catches the student who stopped at the area of the square on the hypotenuse and reported an area where a length was asked for.

## Closing line for the narrator

Two points on a grid already have a right triangle between them. You just have to draw it.
